patient.name: Gareth Doyle
patient.complaint: Painful, red, oozing appendicectomy wound and fever
background: Emergency open appendicectomy 5 days ago for perforated appendicitis
Bus driver from Croydon; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a red, hot, oozing wound a few days after surgery, or 'most likely organism' (Staphylococcus aureus). Watch for pain out of proportion and crepitus pointing to necrotising infection.

points: Gareth, 54, is **day 5** after an emergency open appendicectomy.
The appendix had **perforated**: a contaminated operation.
Since last night his right iliac fossa wound **throbs**.
Nurses notice **yellow ooze** on the dressing and a foul smell.
He feels shivery and off his food.

steps.lead: A wound problem a few days after surgery is an **SSI** until proven otherwise; Gareth's skin flora (**Staphylococcus aureus**) is the usual culprit.
Gareth stacks the risk factors: **diabetes**, **obesity**, **smoking** and **emergency, contaminated surgery**.

visual.title: Where Gareth's wound is
visual.caption: Lanz incision in the right iliac fossa: red, warm and tender around the scar.

points: Wound edges **red, hot and swollen**, 4 cm of spreading erythema.
Pus expressed from the lower end; a **fluctuant** area below it.
Tender only over the wound; abdomen otherwise soft.
No crepitus, no skin necrosis, no blistering.

steps.lead: Every sign fits: erythema, warmth, tenderness, **purulent discharge** and **fluctuance** suggesting a pus collection in the wound.

steps.q: Which layer does Gareth's infection most likely involve?
o: Not an SSI: a wound haematoma
steps.r: Redness, pus and a fluctuant area at the scar with a soft abdomen point to a **superficial SSI** with a small collection. Deep or organ/space SSI would need imaging to show it.

steps.title: Three anatomical types of SSI
head: Type
Layer
Typical clue
Example
rows: Swinging fever, wound may look fine
Pelvic abscess after bowel surgery; septic joint after arthroplasty

steps.lead: Gareth is febrile and tachycardic, so screen for **sepsis**. He has none of the **necrotising** features: no pain out of proportion, crepitus or necrosis.

steps.text: **Pain out of proportion** to what you see, rapidly spreading redness, crepitus or dusky skin is **necrotising soft tissue infection**, not simple wound cellulitis. Do not just give oral antibiotics and review.

steps.lead: Untreated, Gareth's collection could become an **abscess**, delay healing or make the wound **dehisce**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?': a wound swab for a discharging wound, blood cultures if septic, and ultrasound or CT when a deep or organ/space collection is suspected.

steps.q: Gareth has a discharging wound. Which test should be sent first from the wound?
steps.r: A **wound swab** identifies the organism and sensitivities. Imaging is added when a deep or organ/space infection is suspected.

steps.lead: The diagnosis is clinical; Gareth gets a **wound swab, FBC and CRP**. He is febrile and tachycardic, so **blood cultures** go too.

steps.title: Gareth's bloods
steps.text: Raised inflammatory markers back up the clinical picture. Normal lactate: no septic shock.

visual.title: Gareth's CRP
visual.label: Gareth 142
visual.caption: CRP is normally raised for a few days after surgery; a rise on day 5 alongside a red, oozing wound points to infection.

steps.text: CRP is up after any operation. A **second rise** after the first few days, with local wound signs, is what suggests SSI.

steps.lead: The **gold standard** is clinical diagnosis plus **wound culture**, with **imaging** if deep infection is suspected.

steps.q: Gareth's abdomen is soft but the surgeon wants to know how deep the fluctuant area goes. Which is the most appropriate imaging?
steps.r: **Ultrasound** shows a superficial collection quickly at the bedside. CT is chosen when an intra-abdominal (organ/space) collection is suspected.

steps.lead: Gareth's ultrasound shows a **3 cm subcutaneous collection** above the fascia. A swinging fever with a quiet wound would have needed **CT** for a pelvic abscess.

points: Ultrasound: 3 cm subcutaneous collection, fascia intact.
Swab result at 48 h: **Staphylococcus aureus**, flucloxacillin sensitive.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': oral flucloxacillin for wound cellulitis (clarithromycin if penicillin allergic), drainage of a collection, and urgent surgical debridement for necrotising infection.

steps.title: Managing an SSI
nodes: Assess: superficial or deep? Septic? Collection?
Wound care: open, washout, dressings, debride
Antibiotics if cellulitis, pus, deep or systemic infection
Deep, necrotising or organ/space → surgical review, theatre
steps.caption: Source control first; antibiotics alone do not clear a collection.

steps.lead: Gareth is not shocked and the infection is superficial. His **collection is drained** by opening the lower end of the wound.

points: Two skin clips removed; 15 mL of pus released.
Cavity washed out and packed with a dressing.
Daily dressing changes by the ward nurses.
Diabetes team adjust his insulin to bring glucose down.

steps.q: Gareth has cellulitis around the wound and pus. He has no allergies. Which antibiotic?
steps.r: **Flucloxacillin** covers Staphylococcus aureus and is first line for wound cellulitis. Clarithromycin is the penicillin-allergy alternative.

steps.lead: Gareth has **cellulitis and a purulent wound**, so he gets **flucloxacillin**. Prophylaxis at his appendicectomy reduced, but did not remove, his risk.

steps.text: A penicillin-allergic patient cannot have flucloxacillin (it is a penicillin). The notes' alternative is **clarithromycin**.

visual.title: Gareth's response to drainage and flucloxacillin
visual.caption: Drainage plus antibiotics: fever settles and CRP falls within days.

steps.lead: By day 12 the cavity is clean but the wound edges gape. Once infection is controlled, the gaping wound is **re-sutured**.

steps.text: **Necrotising soft tissue infection** needs **emergency surgical debridement** in theatre plus IV antibiotics: it is the one SSI you never 'watch and wait'.

steps.lead: Gareth's care follows **NICE NG125**: prophylaxis at operation, then treatment of the SSI when it appears.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism, why diabetes or smoking raises risk, why prophylaxis is given at induction, or why necrotising infection needs surgery.

steps.lead: Gareth's wound was contaminated **at the time of surgery**, by his own skin and gut flora; **S. aureus** lives on skin, so it dominates.

steps.title: From incision to infection
nodes: Skin or gut flora enter the wound
Poor perfusion and weak immune response

steps.lead: Gareth's **diabetes, obesity and smoking** all reduce tissue perfusion and blunt the immune response, so bacteria take hold and the wound heals slowly.
Gareth's infection stayed **superficial**. An organ/space infection in his peritoneum would have risked an abscess and **systemic sepsis**.

steps.q: Why is a single dose of prophylactic antibiotic given at induction of anaesthesia?
o: It reduces bacterial load when contamination risk is highest
It replaces the need for skin preparation
It treats any existing wound infection
steps.r: The **incision** is the moment of highest contamination risk, so the drug must be in the tissues then.

steps.lead: Gareth's prophylaxis reduced the bacterial load at **incision**; in a contaminated operation it lowers, not abolishes, SSI risk.
Had Gareth's wound shown crepitus and necrosis, this would be **necrotising** infection (polymicrobial or Group A Streptococcus) needing emergency debridement.

steps.text: **Crepitus** means gas in the tissues from gas-forming organisms; dead tissue has no blood supply, so antibiotics cannot reach it. Only **debridement** removes it.

mcq.q: Which is the most common causative organism of surgical site infection?
mcq.r: **Staphylococcus aureus**, because it is so common on skin.

mcq.q: An SSI involving fascia and muscle is classified as:
mcq.r: Superficial = skin and subcutaneous tissue; **deep = fascia/muscle**; organ/space = the organ or space operated on.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests necrotising soft tissue infection rather than simple SSI?
o: Mild erythema at the wound edge
Pain out of proportion with crepitus
mcq.r: **Pain out of proportion**, rapidly spreading erythema, systemic toxicity and crepitus or necrosis.

mcq.q: An intra-abdominal abscess after bowel surgery is which type of SSI?
mcq.r: It involves the anatomical space entered during surgery: **organ/space SSI**.

mcq.q: Which investigation is most useful when deep or organ/space SSI is suspected?
mcq.r: **Ultrasound or CT** shows abscesses and collections that a swab cannot.

mcq.q: When should blood cultures be taken in suspected SSI?
mcq.r: Swab, FBC and CRP routinely; **blood cultures if septic**, ideally before antibiotics.

mcq.q: First-line antibiotic for cellulitis around a surgical wound?
How is wound dehiscence or poor wound closure managed?
mcq.r: The notes state dehiscence or poor closure requires **re-suturing**.

mcq.q: What is done first when a pus collection is found in an SSI?
o: Give oral antibiotics and review in a week
mcq.r: **Drain** pus: antibiotics cannot sterilise a collection.

mcq.q: Why does diabetes increase SSI risk?
o: It causes skin colonisation with E. coli
It impairs tissue perfusion and immune response
mcq.r: Diabetes, obesity, smoking and immunosuppression **impair perfusion and immunity**, so infection takes hold and healing is slow.

prompts.q: What is an SSI, and what are its three anatomical types?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the layer, because it decides the imaging and whether theatre is needed.

points.p: Infection of the surgical wound or operative site after surgery

Presents as cellulitis around the scar.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a 'most likely organism' question after surgery is Staphylococcus aureus.

points.why: Commonest because it lives on skin.
Both impair perfusion and immunity.

points.why: Perforated bowel or appendix carries the highest bacterial load.

prompts.q: How does a superficial SSI present, in history and on examination?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pick out pain, redness, pus and fever a few days after surgery.

points.p: Wound pain, redness, heat and swelling
points.why: Cellulitis around the scar is the superficial picture.
Pus is an indication for antibiotics and drainage.
Fluctuance means a collection to drain.
Delayed healing is also a feature.

prompts.q: Which features tell you it is necrotising soft tissue infection, not simple SSI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pain out of proportion is the trigger for urgent surgery.

points.p: Pain out of proportion to findings
points.why: Often the earliest sign, before the skin looks bad.
Mark the edge: spread over hours is a red flag.
Fever, tachycardia and hypotension.
Crepitus is gas in the tissue.

prompts.q: What are the complications of SSI, and what suggests sepsis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fever, tachycardia and hypotension after surgery with a bad wound means sepsis from the SSI.

points.why: Needs re-suturing once infection is controlled.
Needs drainage.
Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, spreading erythema.
Necrotising infection is the surgical emergency.

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations for suspected SSI, and the gold standard?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: it is a clinical diagnosis; tests support it.

points.why: Gold standard is clinical diagnosis plus wound culture or imaging.
Identifies the organism and sensitivities.
CRP is high after any surgery: look for a second rise.
Ideally before the first antibiotic dose.

prompts.q: When is imaging used in SSI, and which modalities?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a quiet wound with a swinging fever after bowel surgery needs CT.

points.p: When deep or organ/space infection is suspected
points.why: A swab cannot see a pelvic abscess.
Good for superficial wound collections.
Best for intra-abdominal collections after bowel surgery.

prompts.q: What is the stepwise emergency management of an SSI?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: source control (drain, debride) before or alongside antibiotics.

points.p: Assess severity: superficial or deep, septic, collection?
points.why: Decides whether this is a ward or theatre problem.
Antibiotics cannot sterilise pus.

points.p: Wound care: open wound, washout, dressings, debride necrotic tissue
points.why: Dead tissue must be removed.

points.p: Escalate deep, dehisced, necrotising or organ-space SSI: surgical review, theatre
points.why: Necrotising infection needs emergency debridement.

prompts.q: Which antibiotic is used for wound cellulitis, the penicillin-allergy alternative, and when are antibiotics indicated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the classic answer is oral flucloxacillin.

points.why: Covers Staphylococcus aureus.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin.

points.p: Indicated for cellulitis, purulent wound, deep or systemic infection
points.why: A clean wound without these signs does not need antibiotics.

prompts.q: How are SSIs prevented, and how is dehiscence managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: prophylaxis for clean-contaminated operations such as appendicectomy.

points.why: E.g. appendicectomy; given at induction.

points.p: Re-suture a dehisced or poorly closed wound
points.why: Once infection is controlled.

prompts.q: Why do SSIs happen, and why do the risk factors and prophylaxis matter?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: contamination at the time of surgery, helped by poor host defences.

points.p: Bacterial contamination at the time of surgery (endogenous skin or gut flora, or exogenous)
points.why: S. aureus dominates because it lives on skin.

points.p: Diabetes, obesity, smoking, immunosuppression impair perfusion and immune response
points.why: So infection takes hold and healing is impaired.

points.p: Prophylaxis reduces bacterial load at incision, the point of highest contamination risk
points.why: That is why the dose is given at induction, not afterwards.

prompts.q: Why is necrotising soft tissue infection a surgical emergency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: crepitus plus systemic toxicity means theatre now.

points.p: Rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection causing tissue necrosis
points.why: Can spread along fascial planes within hours.

points.p: Polymicrobial or monomicrobial, e.g. Group A Streptococcus

glossary.SSI: Surgical site infection: infection of the wound or operated site after surgery.
glossary.Superficial SSI: Infection limited to the skin and subcutaneous tissue around the incision.
glossary.Deep SSI: Infection extending into the fascia and muscle beneath the incision.
glossary.Organ/space SSI: Infection of the organ or anatomical space entered during the operation, such as an intra-abdominal abscess.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: Gram-positive coccus living on skin; the commonest cause of surgical site infection.
glossary.Group A Streptococcus: Streptococcus pyogenes; a classic single-organism cause of necrotising soft tissue infection.
glossary.Cellulitis: Spreading bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissue, causing redness, heat, swelling and tenderness.
glossary.Erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
glossary.Fluctuance: A boggy, fluid-filled feel on palpation, suggesting a pus collection.
glossary.Abscess: A walled-off collection of pus that needs drainage.
glossary.Collection: A pocket of fluid or pus within tissues or a body space.
glossary.Wound dehiscence: Separation of the edges of a closed surgical wound.
glossary.Debridement: Surgical removal of dead, damaged or infected tissue.
glossary.Washout: Irrigating a wound or cavity with fluid to remove pus and debris.
glossary.Necrotising soft tissue infection: Rapidly spreading, life-threatening infection that kills tissue; needs emergency surgical debridement.
glossary.Crepitus: A crackling feel under the skin caused by gas in the tissues.
glossary.Necrosis: Death of tissue, seen as dusky, grey or black skin.
glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.Clean-contaminated: An operation entering the gut, airway or urinary tract under controlled conditions, such as appendicectomy.
glossary.Contaminated: An operation with gross spillage or acute inflammation, such as a perforated appendix.
glossary.Prophylactic antibiotics: Antibiotics given before infection occurs, usually at induction of anaesthesia, to reduce SSI risk.
glossary.Flucloxacillin: Narrow-spectrum penicillin active against Staphylococcus aureus; first line for wound cellulitis.
glossary.Clarithromycin: Macrolide antibiotic; the alternative for wound cellulitis in penicillin allergy.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein, an inflammatory marker that rises in infection and normally after surgery.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count, including the white cell count.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to detect bacteria in the bloodstream, taken if the patient is septic.
glossary.Wound swab: Sample of wound discharge sent for culture and antibiotic sensitivities.
glossary.Lanz incision: A transverse right iliac fossa incision used for open appendicectomy.
glossary.Endogenous: Coming from the patient's own body, such as their skin or gut flora.
glossary.Exogenous: Coming from outside the patient, such as theatre staff, instruments or the environment.
glossary.NICE NG125: NICE guideline on preventing and treating surgical site infections.
glossary.Polymicrobial: Caused by more than one species of organism together.

technique.stem: A 67 year old woman is 4 days after an elective right hemicolectomy. She has increasing pain at her midline wound. She has type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 36. The wound edges are red, warm and tender with a small amount of pus at the lower end. The abdomen is otherwise soft. There is no crepitus. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a wound a few days after surgery: decide infection or not, then which layer.

clues: type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 36
steps.x: Timing fits SSI; two risk factors; inflammation plus pus at the scar; soft abdomen and no crepitus keep it superficial and not necrotising.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Red, hot, tender wound with pus a few days post-op: **superficial SSI**.

elim: A hernia is a bulge, usually months later, not a red pus-filled wound.
Needs pain out of proportion, crepitus or necrosis and systemic toxicity.
A seroma is clear serous fluid without redness or pus.
A haematoma is blood, bruised and swollen, not purulent.

steps.x: **D. Superficial SSI.** Rule: post-op wound + redness + pus = SSI; add crepitus or disproportionate pain before you call necrotising.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man is 6 days after an open appendicectomy for a perforated appendix. His wound is red and discharging pus. He feels unwell and is shivering. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. A wound swab has been sent.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: Next investigation, with a swab already sent: what else does a septic SSI need?

clues: A wound swab has been sent
steps.x: Fever, tachycardia, borderline hypotension and tachypnoea: he is **septic** from the SSI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Septic patient: **blood cultures** before antibiotics, alongside FBC and CRP.

elim: An abdominal X-ray does not show wound or soft tissue infection.
MRI is slow and not the first test; ultrasound or CT is used for collections.
Procalcitonin is not part of the standard work-up and will not identify the organism.
No urinary symptoms; the source is obvious.

steps.x: **B. Blood cultures.** Rule: swab, FBC, CRP for every SSI; add **blood cultures if septic**.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man with type 2 diabetes is 3 days after an inguinal hernia repair. Over 8 hours his groin pain has become severe, far worse than the mild redness suggests. The redness is spreading rapidly and there is crepitus on palpation with a dusky patch of skin. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 86/52 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Oral flucloxacillin and review in 48 hours

steps.x: Next step in management: decide how dangerous this wound is.

clues: far worse than the mild redness suggests
steps.x: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, necrosis and shock: **necrotising soft tissue infection**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A surgical emergency: **urgent surgical debridement** (with IV antibiotics and resuscitation).

elim: Nothing suggests DVT; delay would be dangerous.
Oral antibiotics cannot reach dead tissue and he is shocked.
Re-suturing is for dehiscence once infection is controlled.
Topical treatment is useless for deep, spreading necrotising infection.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical debridement.** Rule: pain out of proportion + crepitus = theatre now.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman is having a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The anaesthetist gives a single intravenous dose of antibiotic at induction, just before the first incision. A medical student asks why the dose is given at this point rather than after the operation.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason?
o: It reduces bacterial load at the time of highest contamination risk
It sterilises the gallbladder before removal
It treats existing skin colonisation permanently

steps.x: A mechanism question about timing of prophylaxis.
The drug must be in the tissues when the skin is opened.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Prophylaxis lowers the **bacterial load at incision**, the moment of highest contamination risk.

elim: Antibiotics increase, not prevent, C. difficile risk.
Antibiotics have no analgesic effect.
A single dose does not sterilise an organ; the gallbladder is removed anyway.
Skin flora return; prophylaxis is about the operative window.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: prophylaxis works at the incision; clean-contaminated operations benefit most.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man is 5 days after an open right hemicolectomy. He has increasing pain at his midline wound and a foul-smelling discharge. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. The wound edges are red, warm and swollen with purulent discharge. The abdomen is soft away from the wound. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Red, warm, swollen wound with pus and fever on day 5 is a superficial SSI. An anastomotic leak would give peritonism and systemic deterioration, not a soft abdomen with local wound signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a post-operative wound problem.

clues: abdomen is soft away from the wound
steps.x: Timing, a risk factor, pus and a soft abdomen point to infection limited to the wound.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Superficial SSI.**

elim: Leak gives peritonitis and a rigid abdomen.
A hernia is a bulge, not pus.
Seroma fluid is clear, not purulent.
Haematoma is blood and bruising, not pus.

steps.x: **D.** Wound redness plus pus after surgery is an SSI.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman is 7 days after a total knee replacement. Her wound is red and discharging pus. A wound swab is sent. She has rheumatoid arthritis and takes methotrexate. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of SSI because it lives on skin. S. epidermidis is more typical of late, low-grade prosthetic infection.

steps.x: Most likely organism for an early wound infection.
Early, purulent wound infection; immunosuppression raises risk but does not change the commonest organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Staphylococcus aureus.**

elim: E. coli suggests gut contamination, not a knee wound.
Pseudomonas is less common and typical of burns or chronic wounds.
S. epidermidis causes indolent, late prosthetic infection with little pus.
S. pneumoniae is a respiratory pathogen.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: SSI organism = skin organism = S. aureus.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes is 2 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. His groin pain has become excruciating over 6 hours, much worse than the faint redness suggests. The redness is spreading quickly and there is crepitus. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 90/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus and systemic toxicity mean necrotising soft tissue infection. Simple cellulitis or superficial SSI does not cause crepitus or shock this fast.

steps.x: Diagnosis: is this ordinary wound infection or the emergency?

clues: much worse than the faint redness suggests
steps.x: Every necrotising feature: disproportionate pain, rapid spread, gas, shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Necrotising soft tissue infection.**

elim: Cellulitis does not cause crepitus or this degree of toxicity.
DVT gives a swollen leg, not crepitus in the groin.
Superficial SSI has pain in keeping with the signs.
Haematoma is bruised swelling without gas or shock.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: pain out of proportion + crepitus = necrotising.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman is 8 days after an anterior resection for rectal cancer. She has a swinging fever and lower abdominal pain. Her laparoscopic port wounds look clean and dry. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is tender in the suprapubic region.

visual.title: Where she is tender
visual.caption: Deep pelvic tenderness with clean port wounds.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A swinging fever with pelvic tenderness and clean wounds after bowel surgery suggests a pelvic abscess: an organ/space SSI. Superficial and deep SSIs show signs at the wound.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which type of SSI?

clues: port wounds look clean and dry
steps.x: Swinging fever = collection; clean wounds = not superficial; pelvic tenderness = the space operated on.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Organ/space SSI** (pelvic abscess).

elim: Deep SSI involves fascia or muscle under the wound, with wound signs.
Superficial SSI shows red, pus-filled wounds.
The wounds are intact.
Haematoma causes bruising and swelling, not a swinging fever.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: quiet wound + swinging fever after bowel surgery = organ/space SSI.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man is 9 days after an emergency laparotomy for a perforated sigmoid colon. He has had a red, purulent wound for 4 days. This morning he coughed and felt something give. There is now a large pink serous discharge and the wound edges have separated. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Separation of the wound edges with serosanguinous discharge after SSI is wound dehiscence, a complication of SSI that needs re-suturing. A fistula would discharge bowel contents.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a complication of a known wound infection.
Infected wound plus a strain, then pink fluid and gaping edges.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wound dehiscence** complicating SSI.

elim: A fistula discharges faeculent or bowel fluid.
A hernia is a bulge under intact skin, usually months later.
A seroma is a fluid swelling under closed skin.
A haematoma is blood under the skin, not gaping edges.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: SSI weakens the wound; edges apart = dehiscence, which needs re-suturing.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman is 6 days after an open cholecystectomy. Her wound has become increasingly painful and red with pus over 2 days. She is now confused. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her chest is clear and her calves are soft.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hypotension?
o: Sepsis secondary to surgical site infection
practice.e: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension and raised lactate with a purulent wound mean sepsis from the SSI. Haemorrhage would not cause fever and a high white count.

steps.x: Cause of shock after surgery.

clues: chest is clear and her calves are soft
steps.x: Infected wound plus fever, confusion and shock; clear chest and soft calves point away from pneumonia and PE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis secondary to SSI.**

elim: No new drug, rash or wheeze.
Bleeding does not cause fever and pus.
No chest pain; fever and pus explain everything.
PE gives hypoxia and pleuritic pain; saturations are near normal.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: bad wound + fever + hypotension = sepsis due to SSI.

practice.stem: A 48 year old man is 5 days after a laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair. One port wound is red, tender and oozing a small amount of pus. He feels well. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 128/82 mmHg. There is no fluctuance.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Wound swab for microscopy, culture and sensitivity
practice.e: A discharging superficial SSI in a well patient needs a wound swab. Blood cultures are for septic patients, and imaging is for suspected deep or organ/space infection.

steps.x: Initial investigation for a mild wound infection.

clues: oozing a small amount of pus
steps.x: Superficial, discharging, not septic, no collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wound swab** for culture and sensitivities.

elim: Blood cultures are for a septic patient.
CT is for suspected organ/space collections.
MRI is not a first-line SSI test.
An abdominal X-ray does not assess the wound.

steps.x: **E.** Rule: pus at the wound = swab it.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man is 7 days after a sigmoid colectomy. He has a swinging fever and left iliac fossa pain. His midline wound is clean. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
practice.e: Suspected organ/space SSI (intra-abdominal collection) after bowel surgery needs cross-sectional imaging: CT abdomen and pelvis. A swab of a clean wound will not find a deep abscess.

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation: what will show the source?
Classic intra-abdominal collection: organ/space SSI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen and pelvis.**

elim: AXR cannot show an abscess reliably.
Colonoscopy risks the fresh anastomosis and does not show collections.
Erect CXR looks for free air, not a collection.
The wound is clean; there is nothing to swab.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: deep or organ/space SSI = image it (ultrasound or CT).

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman is 6 days after an open appendicectomy. Her wound is red, warm and tender with 3 cm of surrounding erythema. There is no pus and no fluctuance. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Cellulitis around a surgical wound is treated first line with flucloxacillin. Clarithromycin is only for penicillin allergy, and there is no collection to drain.

steps.x: Initial management of wound cellulitis.
Cellulitis around the wound, no collection, no allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral flucloxacillin.**

elim: Nothing to drain without fluctuance or pus.
Clarithromycin is for penicillin allergy.
The wound is intact; re-suturing is for dehiscence.
Topical treatment does not treat cellulitis.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: wound cellulitis = flucloxacillin.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man is 5 days after an open inguinal hernia mesh repair. The wound edges are red and tender with spreading erythema. He had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin as a child. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. There is no fluctuance.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
practice.e: In penicillin allergy, wound cellulitis is treated with clarithromycin. Flucloxacillin, amoxicillin, co-amoxiclav and phenoxymethylpenicillin are all penicillins.

steps.x: Antibiotic choice: check allergies first.
Wound cellulitis in a patient with true penicillin allergy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clarithromycin.**

elim: A penicillin: risks anaphylaxis.
Contains amoxicillin.
First line normally, but it is a penicillin.
Penicillin V: also contraindicated.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: penicillin allergy swaps flucloxacillin for clarithromycin.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman with type 2 diabetes is 6 days after an open umbilical hernia repair. Her wound is red and swollen with a tense, fluctuant 4 cm area beneath it. She has started oral flucloxacillin. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a subcutaneous collection.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Continue flucloxacillin and review in 1 week
Open the wound and drain the collection
practice.e: A pus collection must be drained: antibiotics alone cannot clear an abscess. Re-suturing comes later, once the infection has resolved.

steps.x: Next step, with antibiotics already started.
A confirmed collection: source control is needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Open the wound and drain** the collection, with washout and dressings.

elim: Changing antibiotics does not drain pus.
Steroids worsen infection.
Waiting lets the abscess spread.
Closing over pus traps the infection.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: pus = drain it.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes develops a wound infection 5 days after an open inguinal hernia repair. The registrar explains to the student why these factors increased his risk of infection and delayed healing.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Direct toxicity of glucose to Staphylococcus aureus
Impaired tissue perfusion and immune response
Increased skin colonisation by Gram-negative organisms
practice.e: Diabetes and smoking impair local tissue perfusion and the immune response, which increases susceptibility to infection and impairs wound healing.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why do these risk factors matter?
Both damage microcirculation and blunt neutrophil function.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Impaired tissue perfusion and immune response.**

elim: Glucose does not kill bacteria; it helps them grow.
S. aureus, a Gram-positive skin organism, remains the commonest cause.
Stomach acid is irrelevant to a groin wound.
Neither factor typically lowers platelets, and that would not explain infection.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: poor perfusion plus poor immunity = infection takes hold and heals slowly.
